messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Rajesh Patel is a 58-year-old married South Asian American man who has spent most of his adult life as a bomb disposal technician, a job that taught him to trust procedure, stay calm under pressure, and believe that vigilance could prevent catastrophe. What broke that belief was not an explosion but the months when his young grandson became critically ill with a life-threatening infection and was repeatedly hospitalized. Rajesh remembers the pediatric ICU in fragments that still feel sharper than ordinary memory: the chemical sting of antiseptic in the air, the clear tubing and IV drips, the sight of needles going into a small arm, the monitors beside the bed while adults spoke in urgent, controlled voices. The worst part for him was standing there unable to do anything useful. He could disarm devices in the field, but he could not protect a child he loved from what was happening in front of him.

Since then, reminders in everyday life have begun to seize him without warning. If he walks through a hospital corridor for a family appointment, catches the smell of disinfectant in a clinic, or even sees medical supplies on television, the memory arrives instantly and in pictures: his grandson in the bed, the line in his arm, the metal pole holding the drip. When it comes, it is not a distant recollection but a full sensory reliving that feels real in the moment, as if he is back in that room breathing the same antiseptic air. Being around children can do it too. At work, when a school safety demonstration brings him near a group of elementary students, the sight and sound of small bodies moving around him can abruptly pull the whole scene back.

Those moments do not stay at the level of memory. Rajesh’s body reacts as if danger is present now; he feels a jolt through his chest, his muscles tense, and a wave of fear and dread rises so fast that he struggles to steady himself. He has become especially preoccupied at night, lying awake because he feels he has to stay alert, as though letting his guard down would invite another disaster. The more these reminders provoke that physical alarm, the more he reads his own reactions as evidence that something in him is failing. He has come to believe that a stronger man would have handled this better, and in his darker moments he wonders whether these surges and relived scenes mean he is going crazy.

That interpretation has made the reminders feel even more charged. Rajesh now scans for anything that might set him off, noticing the smell of cleaning products as soon as he enters a building, clocking medical carts and supply cabinets before anyone else seems to see them, and becoming uneasy around children in a way that fills him with shame. Because he has come to believe he cannot stop bad things from happening, each trigger carries more than a reminder of the hospital; it confirms his sense of helplessness. A child’s cough in a waiting room, the glimpse of a needle, the sterile smell on someone’s clothes can leave him thinking not only that the memory is coming back, but that he is the kind of man who freezes when it matters.

The memories themselves deepen that conclusion. When the images slam into him in full detail and for a moment feel completely real, Rajesh takes this as proof that his mind is slipping out of control. He does not experience the reliving as a symptom with a pattern; he experiences it as something happening to him, overwhelming his ability to think straight. Afterward he is left with fear, guilt, and a corrosive conviction that he is weak. Once those beliefs take hold, his nights worsen. He stays awake listening for signs that something might be wrong in the house, telling himself he needs to remain ready, but the prolonged vigilance leaves him more strained and emotionally raw, and in that exhausted state the hospital scenes return even more easily.

Over the past year this has begun to affect his work and family life. In his bomb disposal unit, where he once relied on disciplined concentration, he now finds that encounters with children during community events or the sight of medical kits used in emergency preparedness training can throw him off balance for hours. At home, his wife has noticed that he avoids accompanying relatives to medical appointments and becomes abruptly quiet when grandchildren are playing nearby. What finally brought Rajesh to seek help was a recent episode in a pediatric clinic where the smell of antiseptic and the sight of an IV stand brought the entire ICU scene back so vividly that he had to leave the building, shaking and ashamed. He is frightened most by the thought that he is losing his mind and that, despite a lifetime of training to protect others, he is fundamentally helpless when the people he loves are in danger. He says he wants, more than anything, to be around his grandchildren without feeling his body brace for catastrophe.

violation_explanations: No paragraph clearly states that triggers themselves lead to a sense of current threat or danger, rather than only leading to intrusive memory or physical alarm.
No paragraph clearly conveys that Rajesh’s negative appraisals cause reminders or cues to arise, as opposed to making them feel more charged or increasing scanning behavior.
No paragraph clearly states that intrusive memory leads to triggers or reminders, rather than that triggers bring the memory back.
No paragraph clearly states that Rajesh’s sense of threat or danger leads to negative appraisals, rather than that reminders or memories are interpreted negatively.
